title: Quantum analogue-to-digital converter for phase estimation - Nature Photonics
byline: Caruccio; Eugenio; Roncallo; Simone; Cimini; Valeria; Albiero; Riccardo; Pentangelo; Ciro; Ceccarelli; Francesco; Corrielli; Giacomo; Osellame; Roberto; Spagnol
html:
Abstract

Traditional quantum metrology assesses precision using the figures of merit of continuous-valued parameter estimation. Recently, quantum digital estimation was introduced: it evaluates the performance information-theoretically by quantifying the number of significant bits of the parameter, redefining key benchmarks like the Heisenberg bound. Here we report the first experimental realization of a quantum analogue-to-digital converter for quantum metrology, which takes a continuous parameter as the input and outputs a bit string, using an advanced photonic platform comprising a fully reconfigurable integrated circuit and a quantum dot source of highly indistinguishable photons. We implement a protocol for digital phase estimation that is capable of surpassing classical strategies in terms of mutual information between the output bit string and the unknown parameter, through the simultaneous use of different entangled state resources. We tackle experimental imperfections by using machine learning techniques for noise deconvolution and estimation process refinement. Our protocol is experimentally benchmarked against classical strategies via the number of recoverable bits of the unknown parameter. Our results open new perspectives for future implementation of quantum digital estimation strategies.

Main

Quantum sensors have a fundamental role in several applications, such as atomic clocks and precision timekeeping1,2,3,4, magnetic field tracking5,6 and quantum networks7,8,9,10,11. So far, such sensors have been used as analogue devices. Indeed, quantum metrology protocols mainly focus on continuous-variable measurements, exploiting quantum effects to enhance estimation precision over their classical counterparts12,13. The analogue approaches are well benchmarked using metrics like the root mean square error or the variance. However, with modern instrumentation operating digitally, the interesting metric becomes the number of significant digits at the output. This quantity is measured by the mutual information between the unknown parameter to be estimated and the measurement outcome. A key question is whether the advantages demonstrated in analogue protocols persist in such a framework14, where benchmarking requires different figures of merit instead of traditional ones that—focused on error magnitude or sensitivity to changes—are not appropriate in a discretized domain (for example, due to quantization errors).

In quantum metrology, the standard approach focuses on the scaling of the root mean square error in the number of resources N, and compares it with two fundamental bounds: the standard quantum limit (which quantifies the bound for classical strategies (\(1/\sqrt{N}\))) and the Heisenberg limit (which identifies the optimal scaling for quantum strategies (1/N))12,13,15,16,17,18,19,20. Digitally, these bounds translate into a mutual information that scales as \(\frac{1}{2}{\mathrm{log}}_{2}\left[N\right]\) and as \({\mathrm{log}}_{2}\left[N\right]\) for the classical and quantum scenarios, respectively14,21,22.

In this work, we experimentally implement a protocol for the digital quantum estimation of an optical phase, using an integrated photonic circuit23,24. Our approach leverages the quantum phase estimation algorithm25 as a quantum analogue-to-digital converter (QADC) for phase estimation, which encodes the analogue phase in three bits of information. As probes, we generate a sequence of distinct resource states: a four-photon Greenberger–Horne–Zeilinger (GHZ) state, a two-photon entangled state and a single-photon state. Subsequently, conditional operations are applied to each probe, based on the outcomes of the preceding measurements. To evaluate the protocol performance in terms of mutual information and estimation accuracy, we implement a noise mitigation strategy, taking inspiration from a series of previous works that used machine learning techniques for single and multiparameter estimation problems26,27,28,29. The approach used in this work is different. Indeed, we use a specifically tailored denoising autoencoder (DAE), trained via the ideal probability distribution at the output of the protocol, to deconvolve and reduce the experimental noise. The autoencoder output is subsequently processed by a feed-forward neural network (NN) to mitigate the bias inherent in the estimation process. Within this framework, we demonstrate that the quantum strategy yields a higher number of useful bits compared with the classical interferometric estimation, using an equivalent amount of measured resources.

Results

Protocol

We first briefly review the parallel quantum phase estimation algorithm14. Consider a group of t probes, made of k = 1, 2…2t−1 qubits and prepared in the state \(\left\vert {{\mbox{GHZ}}}_{k}\right\rangle =({\left\vert 0\right\rangle }^{\otimes k}+{\left\vert 1\right\rangle }^{\otimes k})/\sqrt{2}\). Encode the optical phase ϕ ∈ [0, 2π) in \(U(\phi )=| 0\rangle \,\langle 0| +{{\rm{e}}}^{{\rm{i}}\phi }| 1\rangle \,\langle 1|\), evolving each probe with U⊗k. Apply a chain of k − 1 subsequent CNOTs, after which, the kth qubit evolves into \((\left\vert 0\right\rangle +{e}^{\imath k\phi }\left\vert 1\right\rangle)/\sqrt{2}\). Let \(\left\vert m\right\rangle\) label the computational basis of the register made by the least significant qubit of each probe, with size t and state \({\sum }_{m=1}^{t}{{\rm{e}}}^{{\rm{i}}m\phi }| m\rangle /\sqrt{{2}^{t}}\). Taking the inverse quantum Fourier transform (QFT†) yields \(\left\vert {b}_{1}\ldots {b}_{t}\right\rangle\). Measuring in the computational basis provides the binary expansion of the optical phase as ϕ = 2π∑mbm/2m, and thus, the protocol acts as a QADC for the estimation process. We discuss a specific implementation of such a protocol comprising three steps, tailored to the photonic platform design. In this case, the CNOTs chain is achieved by a sequence of Hadamard gates, followed by a controlled σz operation. The QFT†, instead, is implemented without SWAPs30, dividing the experiment in three ordered parts: four-photon, two-photon and one-photon steps, whose outputs control the rotations \({R}_{l}^{-1}=U(-2\uppi /{2}^{l})\) (Fig. 1). An alternative conceptual scheme that uses the same physical device for the phase-encoding step is reported in Supplementary Note 1 and Supplementary Fig. 1.

a, Quantum digital phase estimation protocol consisting of three stages involving four, two and one qubit states, respectively. A unitary operation encodes the phase ϕ in each mode, followed by Hadamard gates and a σz operation, conditioned on the measurement outcomes on the first modes. Depending on the results obtained in the four-qubit and two-qubit steps, controlled phase gates \({R}_{l}^{-1}\) are taken. The bit string {b1, b2, b3} is obtained at the output. Here b3 indicates the higher-precision part of the measurement outcome, that is, the higher-frequency part of the binary expansion. b, Classical interferometric estimation.

Consider the four-photon state \(\left\vert {{\mbox{GHZ}}}_{4}\right\rangle\), evolved by the phase transformation into \((| 0000\rangle +{\text{e}}^{{\rm{i}}4\phi }| 1111\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). Apply Hadamard gates to the first three photons and then measure their parity \(\hat{P}\) in the computational basis, which reads 1 or 0 for bit strings that contain an odd or even number of 1s, respectively. When the parity gives 0, the fourth photon is in \((| 0\rangle +{{\rm{e}}}^{{\rm{i}}4\phi }| 1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\), otherwise apply σz, obtaining the same result. This procedure, which can be implemented in post-selection, is equivalent to the CNOTs chain. Finally, apply a Hadamard gate and a measurement in the computational basis. The output returns b3, the least significant bit of the binary expansion of ϕ.

Consider the two-photon state \(\left\vert {{\mbox{GHZ}}}_{2}\right\rangle\). Due to the phase shift, this evolves into \((| 00\rangle +{{\rm{e}}}^{{\rm{i}}2\phi }| 11\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). Apply a Hadamard gate to the first photon, followed by a computational basis measurement. When this returns 0, the other photon is projected into \((| 0\rangle +{{\rm{e}}}^{{\rm{i}}2\phi }| 1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\), otherwise apply σz. We implement the QFT† adding a rotation \({R}_{2}^{-1}\), controlled by the value of b3, and followed by a Hadamard gate. A measurement in the computational basis yields b2.

Consider the one-photon state \(\left\vert +\right\rangle\). The phase shift gives \((| 0\rangle +{{\rm{e}}}^{{\rm{i}}\phi }| 1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). Apply two subsequent rotations, \({R}_{2}^{-1}\) and \({R}_{3}^{-1}\), controlled by b2 and b3, respectively. Finally, apply a Hadamard gate and a measurement in the computational basis. This gives b1, the most significant bit of the binary expansion of ϕ.

The classical counterpart of our protocol consists in an entanglement-free interferometric estimation. Consider 2t − 1 qubits, all prepared in \(\left\vert +\right\rangle\). After the phase shift, each qubit evolves into \((| 0\rangle +{{\rm{e}}}^{{\rm{i}}\phi }| 1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). Apply a Hadamard gate, followed by a computational basis measurement. For each qubit, the output probability of obtaining outcome 1 is \({p}_{{{\rm{c}}}}(1| \phi)={\sin }^{2}(\phi /2)\). The optical phase reads \(\phi =2\arcsin ({N}_{1}/({2}^{t}-1))\), where N1 is the number of 1s in the output bit string. This protocol shows an ambiguity in [0, π] and [π, 2π], which is typically addressed by introducing and recursively adapting a reference phase for repeated multiround trips31. In our QADC case, this ambiguity is addressed since the measurement outcomes from the group of probes are jointly used for the estimation. Thus, this ambiguity reduces with the number of qubits, for example, to the interval [7π/4, 2π] for t = 3.

In our protocol, post-selection is used both for preparing the GHZ states and at the measurement stage. At the preparation stage, discarded states are irrelevant to the metrological resource count, as they do not carry information about the unknown phase. At the measurement stage, post-selection requires repeating at most 2l times the measurement relative to the bit that requires 2t−l qubits, where t is the number of bits in the outcome. Namely, instead of the number of qubits O(2 × 2t) of the ideal case, where fast feed-forward would avoid post-selection, we need O(t × 2t) qubits, a (moderate) logarithmic overhead. The protocol performance analysis is, therefore, performed on the conditional distribution obtained from successfully detected events.

Experimental implementation

The experimental apparatus, for the implementation of the digital estimation algorithm, is based on a photonic hybrid platform (Fig. 2a). The exploited photon source is a quantum dot (QD) semiconductor, emitting a train of single photons. A 79-MHz pulsed laser is injected in an optical setup tailored to double the pulse repetition rate up to 158 MHz, and then is subsequently used to excite (pump) the QD source at the same wavelength of the energy transition (resonance fluorescence regime)32,33. Single photons are properly discriminated by the pump laser, using a cross-polarization filtering scheme. A time-to-spatial demultiplexer, based on the acousto-optic effect34,35, spatially splits the train of photons into n channels, every 180 ns. Finally, the photon streams are temporally synchronized by fibre delays, and a set of polarization controllers compensate for the relative polarization among the channels. In this way, an n-photon Fock state is produced in the photon spatial degree of freedom. Specifically, the photon numbers required for this experiment are n = 1, 2, 4. Subsequently, the multiphoton state is injected into a universal photonic processor that consists of a fully programmable eight-mode photonic integrated circuit36,37 and a power supply, which provides electrical currents to the chip and allows implementing arbitrary unitary transformations by actuating multiple thermal phase shifters on top of the photonic circuit. The optical circuit comprises 28 Mach–Zehnder unit cells, organized according to a universal rectangular layout38. The unit cell is a reconfigurable beamsplitter composed of two balanced directional couplers and two reconfigurable phases θ ∈ [0, π) and φ ∈ [0, 2π). More specifically, the reflectance R of the reconfigurable beamsplitter is set by tuning θ, whereas φ determines the complex phase of the two-mode transformation. Finally, single photons exiting the interferometer are routed towards a detection stage, which is constituted by superconductive nanowire single-photon detectors and a time-tagging system, having ~42-ps time resolution, which is capable of registering n-fold coincidence detection events. A processing unit is involved in controlling the power supply that sets the currents on the thermo-optic phase shifters, and in recording the detection events coming from the time-tagging system. Further details on the experimental setup are reported in Methods.

Circuit programming and data acquisition are orchestrated by a processing unit. summary: A proof of concept of a quantum analogue-to-digital converter is implemented on an integrated photonic platform, tailored for digital quantum phase estimation in metrology.
